stories.title: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort Review
stories.summary: A collection of sports games designed to spark deceptively heated rivalries.

sources.title: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort Review
sources.text: Back in 2022, Nintendo attempted to revive the fun and charm of the motion-controlled Wii Sports era, but it didn’t quite live up to that lofty goal. Now in 2026, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort takes another swing at that same difficult feat with a clear focus on “more.” More sports, more outfits, more modes, and more collectibles. That doesn't always translate to a better package, with Sports Resort often feeling a wide ocean rather than a deep diving pool, but it more than makes up for it with a broad range of games ripe to bust out at the next big party. So while it may not clear the high bar set by the original Wii Sports in 2006, it still brings out the same child-like joy. Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is a collection of 12 different sports minigames, ranging from highly competitive one-on-one Table Tennis to leisurely cruising in a prop plane around Wuhu Island where they all take place. The quality of each game varies drastically. Archery is a standout thanks to its unique use of the Joy-Con controllers, while a returning sport like Basketball is largely untouched and still feels too choreographed – it's once again missing the freedom of movement and control I want so desperately from a potential party version. The new sports can also be hit and miss. Power Cruising uses two Joy-Con held like you are gipping handlebars to simulate racing a jet ski, but those clunky controls don’t always work well, so it feels more like a gimmick rather than a fun sport. On the other hand (quite literally),Thumb Wrestling helps bring whimsy to the package. It’s extremely silly, but actually makes for some competitive matches – in my online sessions, I was pleasantly surprised with how strategy and tactics changed from match to match. Watching players develop new ways to trick and bait their opponents into getting caught in their trap was entertaining, and I found myself determined to never let anyone get the best of me. Archery is easily the best sport offered in Sports Resort. With four different courses scattered around Wuhu Island, it feels the most well-thought out. I stretched out my arms in front of me, holding both Joy-Con perpendicular to the floor, then clicked the ZL button with my left hand and drew it back to my chest like I would draw a real bow. Using my right Joy-Con to aim at a distant target, it was satisfying every time I hit my mark. More challenging courses and hidden targets to find help flesh out Archery overall, which meant it provided hours of fun for my friends and I in a way many of the thinner options don’t. As you might expect, playing through Sports Resort by myself proved to be a bit lackluster, as it lacks the competitive spirit so intrinsic to the games it recreates. Island Crown, a new mode that has you climb the ranks in nine of the 12 sports, pushed me forward with a little bit of structure and challenge, but even then I found my enthusiasm waning before too long. Its loose story has you defeat challengers in order to eventually face the island champion, who – depending on the sport – will either taunt or cheer you on after every victory. Upon defeating one of the island champions you'll unlock a few more extra objectives in the given sport. Sometimes it's an Island Legend looking for a fight, others it’s a gauntlet of challengers that need to be defeated without losing. It's a decent distraction for those looking to casually play sports while your friends and family aren't around to party, and that’s about it. But when they are around, Sports Resort is easily the game I want to break out. So much of the joy of these games is heightened when folks in the room are cheering, yelling, and getting so into it you need to remind everyone to keep the Joy-Con wrist strap on. This has always been the spirit of the Nintendo Sports games, and Sports Resort is one of the best versions of it around when you've got the crew to play. Recruiting my roommates to run through the sports on a Sunday afternoon was an eye-opening experience. Games like Volleyball – which I found to be incredibly boring during my time with Island Crown and casual single-player – became electric back and forth rallies that lit up the room. Exhausted cheers, disappointing sighs, and questionable calls made even some of the more mundane sports like Golf feel exhilarating.And quick, snappy menus make hopping between sports seamless as well, which kept everyone from zoning out between rounds. Even leisure sports like Skateboarding quickly became heated competitions as we slammed our Joy-Con on the table in mouse mode, ready to race. Skateboarding is the only game in Sports Resort that takes advantage of this control scheme, effectively turning the Joy-Con into a mini Tech Deck. Intuitive controls like flicking your hand to the left or right did 360 pop shuv-its and quickly lifting the front it off the table produced an ollie. With multiple race courses, we ripped through each one attempting to best one another, constantly pushing for faster times as our rivalry grew. My only real complaint about the local multiplayer is that games like Boxing and Power Cruising require participants to have two Joy-Con each, meaning you aren't able to play those sports at all if you only have the single pair that came with the Switch 2. So if you're planning on having folks over to box or ride Jet Skis, ask them to bring some extra controllers. When we needed to cool down, we hopped into the Sightseeing Tour mode, which allows you to zoom around Wuhu Island in search of points of interest marked with giant floating cameras. Collecting a camera marks it on your Sightseeing Log and gives you a little flavor about that part of the island. It's a neat way to get a sense of how all of the sports fit together contextually in this space, and allows you to visit other islanders while they compete on the tennis courts, archery ranges, and more. sources.title: Review Nintendo Switch Sports Resort: a volta a Wuhu Island
sources.text: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort chega ao Switch 2 em 22 de outubro com 12 esportes, a volta à Wuhu Island e gráficos mais caprichados, mas com a mesma experiência de sempre: diversão que rende mais com amigos e família. Testei todos os 12 esportes e conto aqui o que muda, o que apenas volta e para quem o jogo vale a pena. Dá para criar visuais bem diferentes: rosto, penteado, roupas, acessórios e corpo. Os cosméticos são desbloqueados com os pontos que você acumula jogando, e você pode usar o seu Sportsmate ou o seu Mii. O que muda é a forma de conseguir os itens. Você não escolhe o cosmético que quer: o Centro de Itens traz alguns destaques da semana e uma seleção temática (como itens de Halloween neste momento), e cada compra custa 1.000 moedas e sorteia um item. Pode vir de um tom de pele a uma peça de roupa, e a sorte decide. A loja com seleção semanal rotativa já existia em Switch Sports, trocada por pontos de partidas online, então a ideia de uma vitrine que gira toda semana segue a mesma linha. O aquecimento do jogo é apenas o pular corda, que aceita até 4 jogadores e é bem simples. Ele estreia na série: Switch Sports não tinha uma etapa de aquecimento. Vale uma comparação com Fitness Boxing, em que o aquecimento traz alongamentos, exercícios básicos e mobilidade das articulações. A diferença mostra objetivos diferentes: um jogo é voltado ao condicionamento físico e ao emagrecimento, e este é uma experiência de entretenimento. A captura de movimentos dos Joy-Con 2 é precisa, mas há um detalhe que vale considerar: mecânica versus mente. Quando pensamos em esporte, imaginamos os movimentos que aprendemos na escola. Só que alguns esportes aqui são mais mecânicos do que intuitivos, e exigem atenção ao jeito certo de mexer o controle para a resposta sair como esperado. O vôlei é o melhor exemplo. Para saltar e cortar, basta mover o antebraço para cima e para baixo, sem usar o braço inteiro. O instinto é esticar o braço e fazer o corte de cima para baixo, mas o jogo pede apenas um movimento rápido do controle para baixo, algo que dá para fazer até sentado. É um jogo mais acessível por isso, mas que pede um tempo de adaptação. Os 12 esportes são tênis, boliche, tiro com arco, boxe, vôlei, tênis de mesa, basquete, golfe, luta de polegar, avião a hélice, skate e motonáutica. Não há muito segredo em nenhum deles: o que muda é o jeito de jogar, que pede mais atenção. Não cheguei a testar o modo online, então não posso falar do sistema de matchmaking. Ele facilita a vida de quem quer companhia e dos esportes que exigem no mínimo 2 jogadores, e exige uma assinatura ativa do Nintendo Switch Online. O jogo tem o sistema de conquistas e estatísticas e permite enviar figurinhas para os amigos no meio das partidas. São recursos de tradição na série: Wii Sports Resort já tinha cartões de stamps com objetivos, e Switch Sports trazia stamps entre os itens. Na primeira vez que você joga, o jogo pergunta com qual mão você vai jogar, e dá para mudar isso depois nas configurações. Sobre acessibilidade, muitos movimentos funcionam até sentado, o que ajuda quem tem pouco espaço ou limitação de mobilidade. No geral, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort é um jogo de entretenimento, e é assim que ele deve ser encarado. Quem pensa em queimar calorias, como dá para fazer com Just Dance , vai encontrar nos modos mais avançados uma exigência maior do corpo, mas muitos movimentos saem até sentado. Ele não reinventa a fórmula, e quem esperava uma revolução não vai encontrá-la aqui. O que o jogo entrega é a fórmula conhecida, mais completa e mais bonita. Ele chega com 12 esportes desde o início, o que responde à principal crítica a Switch Sports, lançado em 2022 com seis. Quem já conhece a franquia vai gostar das novas possibilidades de jogabilidade, e quem nunca jogou não precisa conhecer os anteriores para se divertir. Quando sai Nintendo Switch Sports Resort? O jogo chega em 22 de outubro de 2026, exclusivamente para o Nintendo Switch 2. Quantos esportes tem Nintendo Switch Sports Resort? São 12 esportes, mais o aquecimento de pular corda: tênis, boliche, tiro com arco, boxe, vôlei, tênis de mesa, basquete, golfe, luta de polegar, avião a hélice, skate e motonáutica. Dá para jogar Nintendo Switch Sports Resort no Switch original? Não. O jogo é exclusivo do Switch 2 e usa os controles Joy-Con 2. Precisa do Nintendo Switch Online para jogar? Só para o modo online. A assinatura do Nintendo Switch Online é necessária para jogar com outras pessoas pela internet. Dá para jogar sentado? Sim, muitos movimentos funcionam sentado, como o corte do vôlei e a esquiva do boxe, que usam apenas o antebraço ou o pulso. Quantas pessoas jogam ao mesmo tempo? Depende do esporte: boxe e luta de polegar são para 2 jogadores, e a maioria dos outros aceita até 4. sources.title: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort Is a Masterpiece
sources.text: The Switch 2 compilation explodes the possibilities of casual gaming as if it was nothing Casual gaming is a term that most of us who are passionate about the video game medium are conditioned to hear as a pejorative. Casual games are superficial, we think reflexively. In trying to please everyone, they're designed for the lowest common denominator. They're shiny and bland, lacking grit and friction. Casual gaming can encompass real beauty, though. It can include PopCap's blissful dopamine machines like Bejeweled , or Regency Solitaire ’s delightfully frivolous mashup of solitaire and Jane Austen . It can also come in the form of 2006's Wii Sports , the fourth-best-selling game of all time, the game that sold 100 million consoles, the game that changed the gaming landscape. Until it didn't. Nintendo's casual gaming era during the Wii and DS days seems like a blip now. Boxed out of its birthright by PlayStation and Xbox and a hardware arms race it didn't believe in, Nintendo, through a mix of desperation and inspiration, found undiscovered country: new players, new ways to interact with games, and a new aesthetic of calm minimalism and self-improvement. But those new players proved tough to cultivate in the long term, and when Switch hit big, Nintendo eagerly ran home to the fans. People were left behind. People like my in-laws, who like video games, who are always game for a bout of Tekken with their grandkids, who play Royal Match on their phones, and whose Wii is still under the TV but hasn't been turned on in years. Casual is a constituency, then, one that's been all but abandoned to the absentee landlords of the smartphone app stores. Casual is also what it says it is: a vibe, a skillfully curated atmosphere. It's relaxed, it's upbeat, it's easy and chill. Everyone is welcome. If casual were a place, it would be Wuhu Island. Wuhu is the setting of Wii Sports Resort , the 2009 sequel to Wii Sports , and now it's back in Nintendo's latest motion-control sports compilation, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort for the Switch 2. Wuhu is a paradise of healthy leisure and sporting spirit, where quirky avatars in colorful outfits compete under crystalline blue skies on golf links of emerald green. The architecture is cleanly modern but also voluptuously curved, and the soundtrack is cheerful muzak, crying seagulls, and constant applause. In Wii Sports Resort , Wuhu Island was a fun backdrop for the usual minigame suite. In Switch Sports Resort , it's a place: an open-world map you can skate on, fly over, and jet ski around. It's like a giant 3D Mario game level, hiding secret caverns and garlanded with thrilling challenge runs. This is Switch Sports Resort 's greatest, but not only, addition to the Nintendo sports canon. There are three vehicle-based sports (amusingly classified as leisure sports, as if everything else on Wuhu was serious business): prop plane, skateboarding, and power cruising (jet skis). In all three, you can freely explore the island in Free Play and hunt for collectables and challenge missions in Sightseeing Tour, as well as participate in competitive races and battles. Free Play and Sightseeing Tour are simple enough sandboxes, yet they revolutionize Switch Sports. They enrich the whole thing by linking the island together into a contiguous location with its own culture and atmosphere. They provide plenty of satisfying, free-flowing gameplay, especially for a solo player. They also open up a new social mood. If you don't feel like competing, you can just hang, skating or flying or jet-skiing around, exploring together and playing freely. At leisure. (My 7-year-old got stressed out by some sports, but we spent ages joyfully doing nothing in skateboarding Free Play.) All three leisure sports are sheer pleasure to control — especially the all-new Skateboarding, which is the greatest application yet for Joy-Con 2 mouse controls. Swipe the mouse back to kick yourself forward, tilt to steer, tip it on to its end for nose or tail manuals, lift to jump, and flick for tricks that grant a speed boost when you land. Hit ZR to slide rasping to a stop, trailing sparks. It's so intensely satisfying. Nobody can match Nintendo's designers for the tactility and invention of their control schemes, and this is one's a peach. Of the nine non-leisure sports, tennis, basketball, and volleyball return from Nintendo Switch Sports , along with the perennial classics, bowling and golf. Archery and table tennis return from Wii Sports Resort , while boxing makes its first appearance since the original Wii Sports . Then there's the all-new thumb wrestling. There's no such thing as the perfect Nintendo sports lineup; bowling and golf aside, it will always be a rotation where a new or returning favorite is balanced out by a sad loss. I mourn Switch Sports ' chambara sword fighting and badminton. Thumb wrestling is good for a laugh, but one of the few sports here without real depth or an interesting alternate play mode. What a joy to welcome boxing back, though, in an interpretation that rejects overexcited flailing in favor of thoughtful and strategic jabs. Archery, too, is magnificent: deeply rewarding to control with a devious multiplayer variant. In the latter, each player is assigned a pie-chart section of the target and presented with an elegant balance of risk and reward: aim for higher points at the center, and you're more likely to land an arrow in an opponent's slice, gifting them points instead. Most sports come with fun variants, like the hilarious 100-pin bowling, or the volleyball rhythm game Bump to the Beat, or table tennis' Return Challenge, in which you have to place returns precisely to knock over soda cans. Playing these is a great way to learn the subtleties of the control schemes — because, like all great casual games, Switch Sports Resort almost invariably hides sophistication within its approachable simplicity. sources.title: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort review: The most feature-packed Nintendo sports game yet
sources.text: Nintendo’s fifth sports game has plenty to offer, whether you care more about solo or multiplayer Next month marks the 20th anniversary of Wii Sports, one of the most influential games in the history of the medium. Whether you got along with its motion controls or not, there can be no denying that Wii Sports scratched an itch with a huge number of people who wouldnât traditionally call themselves video game players. Its 82 million units sold â many of which were bundled with the console in the West, of course â played a major role not only in the Wii becoming Nintendo âs first home console to break the 100 million milestone, but in transforming the shape and typical demographics of the video games audience. Since then, Nintendo has gone back to Wii Sports a few times in an attempt to keep that audience returning. Wii Sports Resort made use of the Wiiâs new MotionPlus accessory, and sold 33 million units as a result. Wii Sports Club on Wii U was less successful (as was practically everything on Wii U), offering an odd digital delivery method where players paid for each sport separately. The series returned after a nine-year break in 2022 with Nintendo Switch Sports , and while it may not have dominated the headlines on specialist video game sites, its 18 million sales showed the series was still no slouch when it came to appealing to the mainstream market after all this time. Now Nintendoâs back â just in time for the 20th anniversary â with the fifth game in the Wii / Switch Sports series, and while itâs still never going to win over the anti-motion control crowd, those who are more accepting of it will find that itâs easily the most feature-packed entry in the series to date. As the name suggests, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort does what Wii Sports Resort did 17 years ago and sets the game on a tropical resort, the returning Wuhu Island. While the various sports on offer take place in venues on Wuhu Island, part of the game also involves exploring the resort itself. There are 12 sports on offer here, consisting mainly of returning classics but also throwing a few new events into the mix. Fans of the original Wii Sports will be happy to see the return of Tennis, Boxing, Golf and Bowling (letâs face it, Baseball was nobodyâs favourite), and they more or less control like they did back in the day. This has its positives and its negatives, as it ever did. Tennisâs simple âswing the Joy-Con to swing the racketâ control method means players of all skill levels can play together, but accuracy is still determined by the same slightly unwieldy method as before, where swinging too early or late would send the ball to the left or right respectively. With no option to move your character using the control stick, or have more control over where your shots go, Tennis still has that odd vibe to it where itâs fun but always feels a little random. Youâll still feel great satisfaction when a shot flies diagonally across the court and lands right on the sideline on the way out, but itâs mixed with the knowledge, deep down, that you werenât fully responsible for that. Five of the other sports â Archery, Table Tennis, Basketball, Power Cruising and Prop Plane â come from the Wii sequel, Wii Sports Resort. Basketball is probably the weakest sport in the game because its dribbling and off-the-ball running controls are clunky, but the other four are among the best. Table Tennis provides the accuracy not seen in Tennis, while Archery originally made great use of the Wii MotionPlus controls back in the day and is still has that âone more goâ factor as you try to hit successive bullseyes over increasingly long and windy distances (not to mention more ridiculous locations, culminating in a round inside a volcano). Power Cruising and Prop Plane, meanwhile, do have competitive elements of their own but theyâre best used for the Sightseeing Tour mode, which Iâll get to in a bit. The final three sports bring the list to a close are Volleyball, Thumb Wrestling and Skateboarding. Volleyball returns from its debut in Nintendo Switch Sports and remains a reasonable enough take on the sport, but itâs probably not one of the more exciting events in the package. Thumb Wrestling is also rather basic but it does at least have a degree of strategy in it. By resting your thumb down you can power it up and make the thumb bigger, but obviously this also leaves you wide open to being âpinnedâ by your opponentâs thumb. It’s simple but it’s also the one I’ve spent most time on so far. This is also the only event in the game which actually features the dreaded w-word, so if you â like me â are a Wii apologist who was bored of people saying every game had waggle in it back in the day, you might want to pretend this one doesnât exist, even though itâs actually fun enough. That leaves Skateboarding, which is the only event to specifically make use of the Switch 2 âs unique controls, specifically the mouse controls on the Joy-Con. In a sort of easier variation on Nintendoâs wheelchair basketball game Drag x Drive , here you use a single Joy-Con in mouse mode and drag it back to speed up, while tilting it to turn It works very well, but itâs perhaps the one event that may have a bigger learning curve for complete novices. My 8-year-old daughter got used to every other sport in the game, but struggled for a while with the Skateboarding controls and asked why she couldnât just walk around the island instead. Which brings me to one of the more entertaining parts of the game, the Sightseeing Tour. There are a total of three different Sightseeing Tours in the game, found in the Prop Plane, Skateboarding and Power Cruising menus, and completing them all will take you plenty of time. sources.text: One of my very favourite things to do in Switch Sports Resort isn't, technically, a sport at all. I can't get enough of Prop Plane's free-play mode, taking to the skies, and watching Wuhu Island do its thing below. Swing past the art museum or the shopping precinct and you'll see all sorts of little people milling around; take a wrong-way dive into a tunnel and here come the cars whizzing on by. Out on the water, racers whip and twirl; on the archipelago's sandiest beaches, holidayers recline in the tropical sun. Fly over the stadiums and sports arenas and you'll see matches in progress - furious bouts of tennis, concentrated swings on golfing greens, or the pin-toppling bustle of bowling - crowds going wild in tandem. And if it's quieter contemplation I want, I can explore the subterranean depths of a volcano, or chart a gently winding path along the river banks, or admire the lighthouse perched on the hill. It's all so extra ; a big, characterful backdrop full of lovely little flourishes that bleed into the games themselves. From the crowds milling lazily along the beach behind the table tennis arena as boats drift on by, to the lovable daftness of it all, as players make hyperkinetic slapstick dashes across tennis courts or glower with teeth-gritted fury in between boxing match rounds. It's just very Nintendo; packed with endlessly delightful incidental touches that help massively elevate what is, in essence, a relatively straightforward and largely familiar collection of sports-themed mini-games. And fundamentally Switch Sports Resort really is more of the same; albeit a further evolution of the hugely influential Wii Sports formula that here, fourth time around, is perhaps at its most refined. Switch Sports Resort brings together a total of 12 activities (13 if you count the rope-jump "warm-up"), and, shorn of its predecessors' filler, it's a strong line-up. You've got four bonafide classics in returning Wii Sports favourites Tennis, Golf, Bowling, and Boxing; five from 2009's Wii Sports Resort (Archery, Basketball, Table Tennis, Power Cruising, and Prop Plane), plus three new additions in Thumb Wrestling, Volleyball, and Skateboarding; all intuitively adapted for Switch 2 's responsive motion controls. And the balance between accessibility and depth feels right. This is a game that favours quickfire arcade-y immediacy over fussy simulation, but still manages to capture the essence of each sport. And as easy to learn as most games are, there's enough subtlety beneath the slapstick silliness to create space for skill, and they adapt equally well to impromptu family chaos and more focused play. The Big Four - Bowling, Boxing, Golf, and Tennis - are, of course, classics for a reason, and they're still winners here. Tennis and Bowling remain the gold standard; the kind of games you can shove into anyone's hand and they'll have a good time, instinctively picking up the nuances of each, the curves and the angles, as they go along (Table Tennis is similarly approachable, although its comparative restraint - trading the giddying arm flails of its bigger brother for subtler wrist action - is a slightly harder sell). Golf and Boxing are a touch more involved - boxing with its upper and lower cuts, its dodge timings and stamina management; golf with its reliance on an on-screen power meter that requires splitting your focus in two - but those hurdles are easily surmountable. And Golf, in particular, with its leisurely pace and less frenetic competition remains a unique sort of low-key thrill. Archery, too, is a blast; its two controller set-up - one for the bow, the other the string - wonderfully mimicking the act of launching an arrow as you pull back, take aim, and fire. Thumb Wrestling is perhaps the dark horse of the bunch; a deceptively simple game of pin-the-digit that quickly descends into psychological warfare as you embark on an increasingly desperate succession of frantic shake-offs and sneaky feints. As for the final two competitive sports on the roster, Basketball and Volleyball, I'm not so keen. Break them down to their constituent parts, and the moment-by-moment movements - the shooting, the dribbling, the jumps, and the bumps - translate well to motion controls. It's just that in trying to adapt both games into something manageably quickfire, it all feels a little awkward - each defensive and offensive phase requiring its own moves you'll switch between like a game of Simon Says. There's no real sense of fluidity and momentum, nor are they easy to explain for casual play. But actually, it doesn't really matter. Basketball and Volleyball, like most games in the pack, come with some properly enjoyable variants, spinning the core of the sport into something new. Basketball's frantic single-player hoop-shooting variant is a brilliantly breathless dash against the clock, for instance, while Volleyball gets a rhythm-action twist, requiring players to bop balls on beat, listening for tricksy musical cues that gets increasingly chaotic as things go on. Bowling, meanwhile, offers the classic 100-pin variant and a fun mini-golf-like spin that challenges players to hit pins while navigating shifting obstacles, massive gaps, and bizarrely undulating lanes. And I particularly adore Archery's special rules. Here, players score points by landing an arrow on a shared target; hit a competitor's area instead of your own, however, and they get the points. More points are earned closer to the bullseye where all quadrants converge, making for some nailbiting risk and reward. Another twist: the better you do, the smaller your quadrant gets, and then come the moving targets and high winds. It's a load of fun. Not every sport and every variant supports four players on a single console (Nintendo, incidentally, has done a decent job of streamlining controller requirements, so you'll generally only need one pair of Joy-Cons for two players, and two sets for four), and not everything is playable online. sources.title: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort é definitivo e tem aura de férias de verão
sources.text: Se tem uma empresa que conhece o seu público como a palma da mão é a Nintendo. A Big N sabe que basta um joguinho descompromissado de esportes para nos trazer memórias dos tempos inesquecíveis de Wii Sports e, mais que isso, nos fazer esquecer que o Nintendo Switch 2 ainda está devendo um novo Mario 3D. Ela sabe, por exemplo, que nem mesmo um colosso como Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, que curiosamente chega junto com Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, seria capaz de ofuscar o lançamento de seu party game esportivo. Por mais que muita gente não ligue para esse tipo de experiência, uma coisa é certa: é o tipo de game perfeito para entreter visitas. Jogos casuais, ou melhor, party games, podem ter uma conotação negativa para algumas pessoas. Se você me disser que não costuma receber amigos em casa tantas vezes quanto gostaria, ou ao menos não o bastante para justificar a aquisição de um game como esse, eu tenho boas notícias: há conteúdo de sobra para quem gosta de se exercitar virtualmente sem companhia. Em Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, somos convidados para passar férias na Ilha Wuhu mais uma vez. O arquipélago paradisíaco debutou no Wii e, desde então, virou cartão-postal dos títulos de esportes da Nintendo, marcando presença até em Mario Kart. Retornar a esse lugar é como voltar para uma antiga casa de praia que nos marcou na infância. Tudo parece igual à primeira vista, mas muita coisa mudou nesse intervalo de tempo em que você esteve fora: o refúgio litorâneo tem ares de renovação. Mais idílica e extensa, sem as limitações de hardware que a impediam de se tornar o playground que poderia ter sido, Wuhu agora se apresenta como um mundo aberto com M maiúsculo. Você seleciona a modalidade que deseja a partir de um menu minimalista, que na hora nos remete à era de ouro do Wii, mas também pode explorar a ilha a seu bel-prazer, seja para participar de corridas, encarar desafios de tempo, coletar itens ou simplesmente relaxar e aproveitar o passeio, tal como em uma boa excursão de férias. Curtir a ilha sem hora para ir embora, como se a rotina escolar ou de trabalho não existisse no dia seguinte, é uma terapia das mais efetivas. Absolutamente todas as modalidades fazem excelente uso dos Joy-Cons do Switch 2 e recorrem a maneiras criativas, algumas até inusitadas, de reproduzir os movimentos característicos de cada esporte. É até difícil explicar: há algo de hipnotizante na combinação dos belos visuais do recanto tropical com a jogabilidade intuitiva dos minigames. Durante o meu período de testes, eu não via a hora de terminar os afazeres para desfrutar dos meus breves instantes de tranquilidade em Wuhu. É como um porto seguro ao qual retornamos quando precisamos desacelerar o ritmo da rotina. São 12 atividades diferentes para experimentar, desde as mais tradicionais, como tênis, boliche e vôlei, até a irreverente luta de polegares. Para quem não se lembra, a rixa de dedo rendeu o melhor meme dos games de 2026 quando o executivo da Nintendo, Yoshiaki Koizumi, demonstrou suas mecânicas, balançando os Joy-Cons freneticamente. Longe de mim insinuar alguma coisa, mas a cena não ajudou a afastar piadas de duplo sentido. Não pretendo destrinchar os aspectos individuais das modalidades, mas gostaria de destacar minhas favoritas (ou as que mais me surpreenderam neste início). Por ter feito parte da minha juventude, era natural que eu me encantasse pelo skate logo de cara. Na verdade, o avião a hélice, a motonáutica e o skate são um espetáculo à parte, já que também servem como meios de locomoção e nos permitem explorar a ilha por céu, mar e terra. No skate, por exemplo, o Joy-Con assume a forma de um shape, e você deve usá-lo como um mouse para remar, mudar de direção e fazer manobras. Arrastar o controle sobre uma superfície plana faz com que o Mii impulsione o corpo e ganhe velocidade. Erguê-lo rapidamente do apoio, por sua vez, executa um ollie, que é a manobra básica de salto. Ao explorar os céus da ilha, por outro lado, seguramos o Joy-Con como um aviãozinho de papel para simular o ato de voar. Não vou mentir: provoca uma certa fadiga muscular manter o braço erguido na vertical, mas é um esforço que acaba sendo recompensado com vistas privilegiadas de Wuhu e uma nostalgia repentina de Pilotwings. Já na água, pude relembrar meus tempos de Wave Race 64, nos anos 1990, enquanto controlava veículos em um mar azul-turquesa, espumoso e aparentemente muito refrescante. A melhor parte de comandar o brinquedo aquático é que a física das ondas é respeitada: elas continuam balançando e podem atrapalhar a pilotagem nos momentos mais inoportunos, o que torna qualquer disputa na praia acirradíssima. Aliás, controlar o jet ski é uma das coisas mais legais que o jogo tem a oferecer: é preciso posicionar as mãos com ambos os Joy-Cons como se estivesse segurando um guidão. Virar exige inclinar os controles na direção desejada, embora demande um esforço ao qual meus antebraços definitivamente não estavam acostumados. Apesar de eu estar dando meu melhor para dar detalhes na análise, Switch Sports Resort é o tipo de jogo cuja sensação de jogar nunca será transmitida por completo, nem em texto, muito menos em vídeo. sources.title: Final Fantasy Resonance review: "A breezy nostalgia-laced JRPG that gives the HD-2D style a shot in the arm"
sources.text: Like Octopath Traveler 0, Final Fantasy Resonance is a rejuvenated way to experience a story once bound and lost to mobile. It may not reinvent the series, but in giving the HD-2D style a much needed upgrade this retro-modern refresh feels like a mainline adventure in its own right. Engaging battles that mix classic and modern Final Fantasy conventions Generous cadence of side quests and challenges CG sequences can jar with HD-2D presentation Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy. Final Fantasy Resonance is at once a nostalgia-laced antidote for the longtime fans who have felt alienated by the recent 3D iterations turning their backs on the series' turn-based traditions as well as Square Enix giving its trademarked HD-2D style a much needed shot in the arm. While I've been enamored by this retro-modern style since its introduction in 2018's Octopath Traveler , over time it's been losing its charm, as the same presentation had been wheeled out in successive nostalgic outings, though at least Dragon Quest 7 Reimagined had the good grace to try something different . Nonetheless, its legacy of pixel-based classics like Final Fantasy 6 meant it was only a matter of time before a Final Fantasy title would receive the HD-2D treatment while also finding ways for the aesthetic to feel fresh again. Ironically, it's done that not through a brand new game but with an adaptation of mobile spin-off Final Fantasy Brave Exvius. My first Final Fantasy was Final Fantasy 8, whereafter I have played through most of the series' mainline instalments, including the 2D classics, as well as its many spin-offs, although Final Fantasy: Brave Exvius had been a blind spot. Using a Nintendo Switch 2 code provided by the publisher, I spent about 40 hours playing through Final Fantasy Resonance, completing all discovered side quests before reaching the credits. – Reviewer Alan Wen Release date: October 22, 2026 Platform(s): PC, PS5, Xbox Series X, Nintendo Switch 2, Nintendo Switch Developer: In-house, Lancarse Publisher: Square Enix Square Enix reworking its mobile catalog to console may not be new, as it has done successfully with Octopath Traveler 0 , and less so with Various Daylife , but Final Fantasy Resonance is more significant as it excavates a since discontinued mobile game. The work from Square Enix Creative Studio 5 and Lancarse is even more extensive than just an act of preservation or removing the gacha elements that had been why Brave Exvius passed me by when it was available . While its story and characters remain intact, the whole presentation and experience has been overhauled to feel like a very classic yet fresh Final Fantasy adventure that stands on its own two feet. Just about everything in Final Fantasy Resonance harks back to the series' classic hallmarks , from turn-based battles with a party size of four characters to the explorable overworld of Lapis peppered with towns, dungeons, random encounters, and – of course – a story that revolves around crystals. As a knight of the kingdom of Grandshelt, your protagonist Rain finds himself setting out on a journey to find the legendary crystals before each can be destroyed by a mysterious group of elite armored warriors calling themselves the Sworn Six. There's plenty that follows a largely conventional structure – visit a new region, discover a problem the locals are having where one of the characters end up joining your party, and a dungeon that culminates in a fight with one of the Sworn Six – but it's not really a criticism when the execution of this formula is done so well. Sure, there are some familiar characterizations, from a leading man obliviously caught in a love triangle, to a feisty mechanic who's often butting heads with the sleazeball of the group, but these are fun characters to spend time with. Even the game's villains are written with pathos, while the series' recurring Espers have their own personality as you fight for the right to summon them in battle. It's all bolstered by the presentation that's a substantial level-up from past HD-2D games. While Final Fantasy Resonance does make use of voice-acting as well as having dialogue text accompanied by expressive character illustrations – the latter introduced in this year's The Adventures of Elliot: The Millennium Tales – its biggest improvement comes from the spritework, which are bigger and feature more animations than what would have been feasible for a 16-bit Final Fantasy. Another subtle yet meaningful shift seen early on is how it's not presented with the same top-down medium-wide camera but actually leverages the fact that the game is made up of 3D environments. It's not that Final Fantasy Resonance strives to be cinematic, but a simple change of the camera to a close-up, more dynamic angles during a boss encounter, or one of your party member's show-stopping Limit Bursts, does a lot to make HD-2D feel fresh again. Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week It's only undermined by the occasional use of CG sequences when you're summoning Espers or Visions, the latter including manifestations of characters from the numbered Final Fantasy titles. Given how their CG sequences are taken straight from Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, I imagine they looked far more spectacular blowing up on your smartphone back in the day. I personally found these transitions at odds with the HD-2D style, and it's perhaps weirder if playing the game with English audio since the CG Visions are only voiced in Japanese. Visions are nonetheless a core component in Final Fantasy Resonance and are significantly overhauled from Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, where they were unlocked through a gacha system. This remake has just 26 from the hundreds of the mobile title but nixes any monetization

sources.text: Alongside Square Enix’s Pixel Remasters and other HD-2D games, Resonance isn’t an essential experience Final Fantasy Resonance doesnât really have to do anything new. This is a new adaptation of an older mobile game, Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, with the gacha system removed and progression completely reworked to befit a more standard, single-player, premium JRPG. Those are all points in its favor, and Resonance evokes the atmosphere and spirit of classic Final Fantasy, but itâs still an adaptation of that older mobile game. Resonance is set in a Final Fantasy world thatâs familiar, but not the same as the ones youâve played before (unless youâve literally played Brave Exvius). Armor-clad knights, elemental crystals, spirits, and summons. Everything about the setting, character designs, and major story beats feels cherry-picked from classic FF games that fans are nostalgic for. Thatâs not necessarily a bad thing. Final Fantasy games have a unique vibe that other long-running JRPG series just canât quite muster, and Resonance manages to evoke that atmosphere even when some numbered entries struggle to do so. On the other hand, this familiarity makes it difficult to connect with the cast when their archetypes shine through more strongly than their own personalities. I quite like the protagonist duo of Rain and Lasswell. Rain is boisterous and doesnât have the gentlemanly qualities of most knights, but is an innately talented warrior. Lasswell, meanwhile, picks up the slack to ensure his adopted brother Rain can rise in the ranks and let his talents shine. But while Lasswell is a more interesting character, he has to give way to Rain, who has unique magical abilities he doesnât understand the origin of. Aside from one major exception, most of your party members are downplayed by the plot past the chapter in which theyâre introduced. Lid is incredibly charming when you first meet her, but past that point her character moments are few and far between. Nicholâs introduction is intense and emotional, but once itâs over, it feels swept under the rug. Past that point, theyâre functional party members that give you more options in battle, and rarely more than that. The major defining feature that sets Resonance apart from other FF games is the Vision system. Youâre able to equip a Vision to each party member, and this Vision takes the form of another character from across the Final Fantasy pantheon. Upgrading Visions gives you access to more of their attacks in battle, and you can freely choose between your own characterâs pool of skills or their equipped Visionâs. Keeping a Vision equipped will enable you to level up a characterâs synergy with it, allowing you to equip abilities and skills from that Vision permanently. Itâs like a hot-swappable job system. If you feel one of your characters needs more curative skills, then you can equip them with a White Mage Vision. If you need access to Water and Thunder element attacks, then teaming up with Cloud Strife is a good idea. There are dozens of characters from different FF games available to unlock and equip as Visions â protagonists and final bosses alike â and this acts as the gameâs main hook. Swapping through Visions, increasing synergy across the cast, and building your main party members to be as capable as possible. “There are dozens of characters from different FF games available to unlock and equip as Visions â protagonists and final bosses alike â and this acts as the gameâs main hook” When collecting Visions from the various Sanctums of Light across the land, you complete a quick three-step quiz to see how well you resonate with the Vision youâre summoning, and the questions are worded so obviously that youâll probably understand what the correct answers are without ever playing the game the Vision is from. Itâs obviously an improvement over Brave Exviusâ gacha system, but these moments feel somewhat cheap, evoking nostalgia for better games. It makes sense for a mobile title, but as a premium game it falls flat. Still, Visions do a lot to spice up a battle system that is otherwise tried and tested. Itâs a traditional turn-based affair with a basic attack, each characterâs own skills, and those of your equipped Vision. You also get access to Limit Break abilities, and modifiers that allow you to build LB more quickly. The final piece of the puzzle is summonable spirits, called Espers, that act as a fifth party member for a short time in battle before unleashing a final strike on your enemies. Otherwise, youâll be using familiar Final Fantasy strategies such as using Protect and Haste to strengthen your team while staggering and damaging foes. Itâs impossible to get lost in Resonance thanks to a map which constantly shows where your next main objective is, along with any side quests youâve picked up. Side quests can offer decent rewards â including some nice upgrades for Lidâs Mecha Chocobo â but by and large theyâre pretty dull, often having you backtrack a bit through an earlier dungeon to witness a new scene or collect an item. Resonance successfully evokes the vibes and atmosphere of Final Fantasy, sure, but it doesnât live up to its inspirations. The battle system and Visions are the standout features, and even they arenât any kind of revolutionary, being broadly bettered by other HD-2D titles from Square Enix . Many of the minor qualms and complaints arenât because of any lack of talent on the behalf of the developers, I think theyâve done a great job adapting a mobile game into a premium title. But the design of its mobile origins limits this gameâs ambitions. Resonance, if it were a truly original title, couldâve been a bigger, bolder celebration of Final Fantasyâs history. sources.title: How Final Fantasy Resonance uses Visions to change how we see the series
sources.text: From Cloud to Zidane, get a deeper insight into the RPG’s gameplay transforming cameos. With its cinematic HD-2D visuals and flashy combat, Final Fantasy Resonance was already piquing the interest of turn-based RPG fans, but its powerful and fun Visions mechanic has really captured the imagination. I went hands-on with the final game to take a deep dive into what Visions are, how they work, and how they transform main characters Rain and Lasswell’s quest to save their world. If you’re familiar with summons in turn-based RPGs, then that’s a good starting point for Visions – but you’ll get a particular kick out of them if you’re a long-time Final Fantasy fan. As I explored Lapis, I encountered crystal shrines that each welcomed me to engage with a short tale of a hero from previous games in the series. After an introduction with video clips and multiple choice questions relating to the chosen Vision, I was gifted with a combat-ready assist companion that could be equipped to one of Final Fantasy Resonance’s main party members, granting different magic and attacks in combat, but also permanently enhancing baseline stats like health and speed. All of which I’ll delve into a bit later, because let’s get into the most pertinent question first… With so many legendary Final Fantasy heroes spanning 16 main numbered titles, series veterans will be pleased to know that a staggering 26 companions are available to find across the entire game. These range from iconic villain Sephiroth (Final Fantasy VII) and amnesiac rebel Terra (FFVI), to the first Warrior of Light (Final Fantasy) and stoic battler Lightning (FFXIII). There’s also a handful of original characters from the game Final Fantasy Resonance has adapted and enhanced here, Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, such as Black Mage Tronn. While most don’t typically talk outside of combat chatter, each legacy Vision feels and looks exactly how you’d want them to, complete with animations and music appropriate to the titles they’re originally known for. And yes, their attacks are just as faithful as well. When a Vision is first awakened I immediately gained access to a basic suite of passive perks, as well as magic and physical strikes to unleash in battle. Take Noctis (FFXV), for example. His opening passive benefits are a 20% boost to my character’s attacks, and the ability to cast Thunder or Blizzard in combat. However, as each equipped Vision earns mastery points from winning battles, more bonuses and Vision specific abilities are unlocked. In Noctis’ case, his early mastery bonuses include a 40% increase of the equipped party member’s limit burst gauge – the special meter that fills over the course of a fight and lets you deliver a powerful single attack – each time you defeat an enemy. Unlocking further mastery levels for someone like Zidane (FFIX) means gaining access to his Steal skill, which can be boosted further with his Mug ability which adds potential damage to his theft attempt. But by far the most spectacular use of a Vision’s power is their Resonance capability. By staggering all opponents during combat – finding their weakness and depleting their stagger meter – I was given the choice of using any of my equipped Visions’ dazzling cinematic finishers, such as Cloud’s (Final Fantasy VII) brutal Ascension Resonance. Let’s not get it twisted – Visions may initially look like regular summon attacks, but there’s far more to them than just that. In fact, Final Fantasy Resonance has more traditional summons in the shape of Espers who can join your battles for a set number of turns. No, Visions fundamentally alter and personalize your party’s proficiencies in combat. The more a party member uses a Vision, the greater their level of affinity grows, which in turn means more bonuses for that character. And because each Vision has a specific role/job status where they excel, I quickly learned to mix and match them to my party characters to either create specialists or all-rounders. For example, Lasswell has the role of a Breaker, a class geared towards staggering enemies in combat. But coupling him with original Vision Medic Leah gave him the ability to use healing magic and an option to pass his combat turn to an ally, which made him my durable back-up support character if my main heavy hitter went down in battle. Allying him with Cloud (also a Breaker) later on gave my version of Lasswell even stronger offensive capabilities to keep him in the fight. Similarly, when Lid joined my party, I teamed her up with Zidane, knowing his Saboteur skills to disrupt and debuff enemies would make Lid a tricky and versatile opponent when combined with her damage dealing Commando skill set. In short, my characters adapted over time to suit my playstyle, but the game never locked me into taking one specific route for their growth, meaning I could evolve them to match the challenges of my quest. And by collecting magicite during the adventure and visiting the somewhat eccentric Moogle of Light, I could increase the base rank of each Vision and unlock even more abilities. Of course, Final Fantasy Resonance isn’t just about Visions, even if they’re a crucial part of the game. From its sweeping orchestral score which borrows classic cues from previous titles, to its globe-trotting and occasionally dark tale, there are plenty of traditional elements that will keep fans happy. And yes, you can still whistle for a Chocobo ride, complete with everyone’s favourite theme tune. How will you customize your characters when Final Fantasy Resonance launches on PlayStation 5 on October 22?

sources.title: Final Fantasy Resonance Is a Missed Opportunity for Square Enix
sources.text: The first HD-2D entry in Square Enix's beloved RPG franchise is big on nostalgia and little else When asked what defines the series he created, Hironobu Sakaguchi is reported to have said , “Final Fantasy is Final Fantasy if it has a blue window with text in it.” It’s a tongue-in-cheek answer that speaks to the certain je ne sais quoi of Square Enix’s legendary RPG franchise. There is, however, something far more important that defines it: crystals. By that barometer, Final Fantasy Resonance is not only a Final Fantasy, it is the most Final Fantasy. It has so many crystals. Resonance , co-developed by Square Enix and Lancarse, is so overtly an homage to every other game that bears the Final Fantasy name. It is packed to the brim with Easter eggs, references, and illusions to what came before it. This is largely a holdover from the game's source material, the now shuttered mobile title Final Fantasy Brave Exvius . Much like Octopath Travel 0 before it, Resonance seeks to strip away the predatory gacha mechanics of the game it was built on and offer up a more streamlined big box title complete with a fresh coat of paint. This, however, only highlights the core issues of the base experience, namely how much of it relies on reminding the player of games that came before it. Nostalgia may have succeeded in getting Brave Exvius players (of which I myself was one for a couple years) to spend real world money on beloved characters, but it falls flat in Resonance . The game is not only in the shadow of the series' past, but also the shadow of more qualified modern successors to the throne that don't have the luck of bearing the all-important franchise name. It is a game with several flaws that franchise fans will likely be able to overlook to appreciate the handful of moments that manage to work just right. That too is quintessentially Final Fantasy. Resonance begins as so many early games in the legendary RPG series do. The world’s many magical crystals are threatened by a great evil and a gang of plucky heroes must put a stop to it. Along the way they’ll laugh, cry, and learn that the greatest power of all is love; a mission best accomplished by going on a sick road trip with your best buddies. The proper nouns of the story are new (the protagonist is named Rain, a weather-appropriate spiritual successor to Cloud and Lightning) but the overarching strokes are familiar. So many plot beats can be directly traced to similar moments from past entries in the series. Two knights that lead an airship? Final Fantasy 4 . An amnesiac girl with a powerful affinity to Espers? Final Fantasy 6 . The list goes on. A story that relies on tropes can be accused of being lazy, but there is a reason tropes exist in the first place — they work! Resonance largely employs tropes to its benefit. It swaddles the player in a comfortable blanket of familiarity that may be predictable but is never unsettling. This aversion to risk feels like a holdover from Brave Exvius , which Resonance only retells the first season of. The paramount goal of a gacha game is retaining players and extracting as much money from them as possible. Narrative swings could affect the player base and, by extension, profit. That means there are few lows in the story, but few highs. That isn’t to say there are no highs. When Resonance ’s narrative occasionally finds its rhythm, it can offer some wonderful emotional catharsis. A standout moment centers around an Aerith/Yuna-like priestess who balances the weight of duty with the desire to live for herself. Combat is turn-based, though it does not use the series' now-signature ATB system. Instead, battles are focused on turn order and using elemental weaknesses to stagger enemies ( Final Fantasy13 ’ s most enduring contribution to the series). It’s engaging enough but lacks a sense of urgency or real innovation that is on display in Octopath Traveler’s excellent boost-break system . The jump from mobile removes something Brave Exvius actually did quite well: By utilizing the touch interface of mobile devices, players could chain attacks and hit enemies simultaneously. It’s a major loss and one of the various ways in which I am constantly reminded that Resonance is not an improved or better game than Brave Exvius by default. Sacrifices had to be made. sources.title: Players on Steam so far seem delighted with Modern Warfare 4's campaign, making it one of the most well-received Call of Dutys in recent history
sources.text: It may be hard to believe, given all the Call of Duty: Modern 4 pre-launch community drama and the beta's lower-than-expected numbers on PC , but the final game may have turned things around - so far, at least. On Steam, Infinity Ward 's final chapter in the Modern Warfare sub-series currently has a Very Positive (92 percent) rating based on over 3,100 user reviews . Modern Warfare 4's campaign early access went live Friday, and the review rating has been improving steadily as players have experienced more of the campaign's missions. Many have likely finished it by now; the campaign is a little over six-hours in length, after all. Gaining access to the campaign on Friday required pre-ordering any of the game's editions digitally. Modern Warfare 4's official release isn't until 23rd October, which makes it hard to determine the current number of players, because SteamDB , our source for this data, can't reveal numbers without its tracking bot having a copy of the game. Setting aside player numbers, the sentiment around Modern Warfare 4 is considerably more positive at the outset compared to last year's Black Ops 7, currently sitting at Mostly Negative (37 percent) . While review ratings change over time with each major update, Modern Warfare 4 is currently the highest-rated Call of Duty in over a decade. However, it's worth bearing in mind that the people playing the game are likely the series' most keen players, so perhaps they're more lenient towards it. We haven't had a chance to review the game yet, having only received code late last week, but IGN published a COD: Modern Warfare 4 campaign review on Friday, scoring it 8/10. In the rebooted Modern Warfare series, the 2019 Modern Warfare game comes closest in average player sentiment with a Mostly Positive rating (79 percent) . 2022's Modern Warfare 2 is far lower with a Mixed rating (45 percent) . Outside of Infinity Ward's output, Black Ops: Cold War is close at Mostly Positive (79 percent) . Modern Warfare 4's next big moment is the anticipated release of DMZ, the game's extraction shooter mode. Like the campaign, DMZ is available early for pre-orders, unlocking tomorrow, 20th October . Finally, on 23rd October, traditional multiplayer becomes available, which is when we're likely to see a shift in user sentiment, if one is going to happen.

sources.title: Frozen Trail finally puts the 'raid' in Arc Raiders
sources.text: The Fallen Emperor and Arc Frigate have me excited for the game's future. Welcome to Play This Right Now, the site version of our weekly newsletter in which we celebrate a new game, update, or DLC that we think is well worth checking out. You can subscribe to the newsletter at the link if you want to get our thoughts about a new videogame happening direct to your inbox every Thursday. I'm standing on top of a flying fortress hundreds of feet in the air, as around me, 15 or so players wage a losing battle against a swarm of flying robots armed with rockets and lasers. It's utter chaos. We fight further and further into the ship, unlocking platforms, defeating waves of enemies and giant turrets which pop out of the deck to gun down unsuspecting looters. But I think we're done. Time is running short and we've once again stalled at this stage of the puzzle. All that's left now is to try and make it back to ground in one piece and live to attempt another day. This is the Frigate , one of Arc Raiders two new raid-style activities, and it's exactly what the game needed. Rather than content you can complete the day the update comes out, Frozen Trail 's Frigate and Fallen Emperor represent a deeper loot chase, tied into upgrading the new outpost and workbenches to fashion special weapons which fire explosive bullets or incendiary grenades. More than that: they're properly fun . I've raided a lot in Destiny 2, completed its dungeons more times than I can count (including soloing some) and I'm quite impressed with the variety of these endgame challenges, how they demand cooperation from players, but also really tie into the features and loot chase that Frozen Trail added. While the Arc Frigate is a pitched battle blasting endless waves of robots as you try to unlock its cargo hold with a bunch of other raiders, the Fallen Emperor is more of an individual challenge. This series of mostly randomised encounters sees you solving puzzles and painstakingly platforming your way through its labyrinth of hazards and Hydra turrets, which love to pick you off when you're dangling in some precarious position. It's a race to perpetrate a bank heist in the corpse of a colossal robot, and if that doesn't get your juices flowing, I don't know what will. Part of the fun is Frozen Trail's new Grappling Hook item, an easy to craft traversal tool that lets you scale and swing in a much more enjoyable way than the game's existing Snap Hook—I always carry one now, just for ease of exploration. The Fallen Emperor is also smart in terms of loot, designed like a kids' gameshow (did anyone here watch Jungle Run?). Players who want the guaranteed big score at the end are incentivised to rush there, lest another raider beat them, but since there are loot containers between each encounter and concealed in them, other players can filter in and still have a chance at getting rare items and rewards for encounters without making it to the end. Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team. The same goes for the Arc Frigate—it's not just about who gets there first; these encounters are layered with loot, and often reward exploration as much as pushing for the end goal, especially as the new upgrades require a wide range of materials. Though Frozen Trail has its bugs—my reward pass still isn't fixed—this is such a positive update for the game's direction. If the PvE-mode test is anything to go by, we'll soon be able to play Arc Raiders' endgame events like the Fallen Emperor, Frigate, Matriarch, or Harvester without fear of getting ratted and having our loot stolen while we're trying to fight big arc, work together, and puzzle stuff out. I'm not a player who minds PvP or the way it elevates the tension and excitement of the extraction shooter genre, but I think there's a good case to be made for a PvE-only option when running PvE-centric endgame events, which often require cooperation. It's also uniquely frustrating getting ambushed after successfully completing one. This happened to me after landing a huge loot haul on the Frigate and basically being the only raider to make it out alive—I was riding high, I wasn't cautious, and of course some punk with a Kettle was waiting at extraction. He even said "Hello" before he ratted me. It's a sucky way to end these cool events and it dissuades players from investing in their challenge, so hopefully any eventual PvE mode that does appear will include these. Still, these new raid-style events have me so excited for the future of Arc Raiders. I can't help but fantasize about how fun and rewarding a Destiny 2 length raid in Arc Raiders would be, or something similar to Building 21 or Koschei Complex in DMZ—a dedicated mode with its own timer, challenges, and bosses. I can't wait to see what endgame content Embark cooks up next. When not scouring games for secrets or bashing his head against puzzles, you'll find him revisiting old Total War campaigns, agonizing over his Destiny 2 fit, or still trying to finish the Horus Heresy. sources.title: Arc Raiders player numbers hit a six-month high following the release of the extraction shooter's huge Frozen Trails update
sources.text: Arc Raiders is still going strong almost a year after finding viral success, and it's all thanks to Embark Studios' one-two-punch strategy of launching a huge new update, Frozen Trails, to coincide with a free weekend. Arc Raiders' Frozen Trails update upgraded the extraction shooter to version 2.0 earlier this month - 8th October - and quickly led to a surge in Steam players interested in its tense PvEvP shootouts. A new report from Alinea Analytics ' Rhys Elliott now claims a similar resurgence took place across all platforms where the game's available. According to the report, Arc Raiders' comeback peaked with a whopping 1.7m daily players jumping in on the 14th of October, its biggest player count in six months, mostly driven by the aforementioned update. What's perhaps most interesting is that player numbers actually peaked just after the game's free trial weekend ended on 12th October - though around 150,000 new looters reportedly joined the robo-infested wasteland during that weekend period. Both events coincided with the game's steepest discount yet, slashing its price tag by 50% to $19.99. In the three days after the free trial, Arc Raiders sold another 150,000 copies and brought home roughly $3m, not counting microtransactions, per the report. Embark Studios' seemingly went all out this month. Frozen Trails itself nudged almost every corner of the game, adding a new map, new weapons, new menacing mechs and much more. A PvE test also tried to accommodate the game's surprisingly friendly community between the 13th and 20th of October. Executive producer Aleksander Grøndal recently said the team isn't against the idea of permanently splitting Arc Raiders' PvEvP gameplay into PvE and PvP pockets . Who knows? Doing so could open the door to another resurgence if done well. Earlier this month, we learned the production company behind this summer's big screen horror hit, Backrooms, is working to adapt both Arc Raiders and The Finals into film and TV projects . Developer Embark is involved, too.

sources.title: 8 melhores jogos de Star Wars que deixam você ser um Jedi
sources.text: Temos certeza que praticamente todos os fãs de Star Wars já sonharam com a possibilidade de empunhar um sabre de luz um dia. Enquanto na vida real temos que nos contentar com meras réplicas, no mundo dos games podemos tornar o sonho de virar um Jedi em realidade. Há muitos jogos que nos permitem reviver eventos famosos da saga de George Lucas, enquanto outros nos trazem histórias e personagens totalmente inéditos. Por isso, nós reunimos os 8 melhores jogos de Star Wars que deixam você ser um Jedi , seja lutando no chão com seu sabre ou pilotando um X-Wing pelos ares. Confira! Sabemos que há inúmeros jogos que realizam essa fantasia, então tentamos selecionar uma lista mais diversa e apenas com jogos de qualidade inspirados na franquia. Lançado em 2019 pela Respawn Entertainment, em Fallen Order , você controla Cal Kestis, um jovem Padawan que sobreviveu à Ordem 66 e vive escondido , trabalhando em um ferro-velho. Quando sua identidade é exposta, ele precisa fugir do Império e continuar seu treinamento. O combate é um dos grandes destaques, já que exige paciência e leitura do adversário. É claro que também há os poderes da Força, como empurrar e frear inimigos , para complementar o arsenal. Tudo ajuda a te fazer você se sentir como um Jedi em formação. Star Wars Jedi: Survivor , lançado em 2023, se passa mais ou menos 5 anos depois e mostra um Cal mais experiente, mas também mais sobrecarregado pelas consequências de suas escolhas. A história ganha um tom mais sombrio e maduro, e o mundo é maior, com destaque para o planeta Koboh. Survivor melhora o sistema de combate com várias posturas de sabre, entre elas a de sabre duplo, sabre cruzado e a combinada com blaster . Cada uma muda o ritmo das lutas e abre espaço para estilos diferentes. É um dos jogos mais completos já feitos sobre a vida de um Jedi e para muitos fãs é um dos melhores exemplos atuais do gênero. Lançado em 2011 pela BioWare, The Old Republic é um MMORPG que se passa milhares de anos antes dos filmes , numa época em que a República e o Império Sith disputam a galáxia. O jogo permite criar seu próprio personagem e escolher entre classes de Jedi ou de Sith. O grande diferencial é a ênfase na narrativa. Cada classe tem uma história própria, com diálogos dublados e decisões que afetam o desenrolar dos acontecimentos. Além disso, é possível jogar com outras pessoas em missões cooperativas, enfrentar chefes e explorar planetas lendários. Lançado em 2003 pela Raven Software, Jedi Academy é um dos favoritos dos fãs até hoje . Você controla um aluno e o treina na academia de Luke Skywalker, aprendendo o caminho da Força sob a orientação de Kyle Katarn. O jogo se destaca pela liberdade de personalização. Você escolhe o formato do sabre, a sia cor e entre os estilos de luta que o jogo oferece. O sistema de poderes ainda permite combinar habilidades do lado do bem e do lado sombrio . Fora isso, há o modo multiplayer que ainda conta com uma comunidade ativa com vários mods e servidores. Este Battlefront II , da Pandemic Studios, não é focado em ser um Jedi logo de início, mas oferece momentos memoráveis para quem gosta da saga. Após alguns tiroteios mais normais, você pode participar das grandes batalhas no papel de personagens como Luke Skywalker , Obi-Wan Kenobi, Yoda, Mace Windu e Darth Vader. O ponto alto é a campanha, que acompanha a ascensão do Império a partir da perspectiva da 501ª Legião , e o modo Conquista Galáctica, que combina estratégia e ação. Ver um Jedi cruzando o campo de batalha, desviando de rajadas e derrubando adversários com a Força é algo que o jogo fez com mais charme do que muitos títulos posteriores. Merece a lista pela diversão e pelo valor nostálgico. Lançado em 2008, The Force Unleashed apresenta Starkiller, o aprendiz secreto de Darth Vader . A trama se passa entre os Episódios III e IV e mostra o que aconteceu enquanto o Império caçava os últimos Jedi. Nesse jogo, dá para fazer muita coisa, já que você pode arremessar inimigos para longe, destruir estruturas, levantar caças TIE do chão e disparar raios com uma intensidade quase absurda . Na época, o motor de física permitia que objetos e inimigos reagissem de forma realista a seus golpes, o que tornava os combates muito mais dinâmicos. Sabemos que geralmente os Jedi estão lutando diretamente com seus sabres, mas não dá para negar que eles também possuem habilidades incríveis em combates áereos . Esse título de GameCube é ainda mais incrível que o seu antecessor, do N64, e te coloca para reviver algumas das batalhas mais importantes contra o império. Para quem quer algo diferente dos jogos usuais de Jedi , esse é um dos melhores da lista. Além disso, é um dos títulos que melhor recriou diversas batalhas e situações icônicas dos filmes. Lançado em 2003 pela BioWare, Knights of the Old Republic costuma ser um dos mais citados quando se fala de jogos de Star Wars. A história se passa cerca de quatro mil anos antes dos filmes e coloca você como um soldado que descobre ter sensibilidade à Força e se torna um Jedi em meio a uma guerra contra os Sith. O sistema de combate pode ser meio datado hoje em dia, mas o resto vale muito a pena. A trama e os personagens são incríveis, sendo que as escolhas de diálogo e das suas ações empurram o personagem para o lado do bem ou para o sombrio. Apesar da idade, continua sendo uma das melhores formas de viver a jornada de um Jedi. Gostou de conhecer alguns dos melhores jogos de Star Wars que deixam você ser um Jedi?
